briefs.preg-vax:
Vaccines in Pregnancy

choosing the vaccine or immunoglobulin due now · the Tdap window optimizes protection; it is not an eligibility gateWhich one is due now, and is this window a gate or an optimization?

What is dueAnti-DVaricellaPractice
Bottom line

The patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins; give the one that is due now. A date, a gestational age or a serology decides which one is due, not a symptom.

  • Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis): every pregnancy, irrespective of prior Tdap; optimal at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably the earlier part, although Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy.
  • The window is an optimization, not a gate: for a wound needing tetanus prophylaxis or a community pertussis outbreak, give Tdap then; a dose given earlier in pregnancy is not repeated at 27 to 36 weeks.
  • Inactivated influenza vaccine: any trimester while flu viruses circulate; in the first or second trimester, preferably September or October; in the third trimester, July or August can be considered. The classic visit is in mid-September, so it is due.
  • Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine: one dose of RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF; Abrysvo, the only one for pregnancy) at 32 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks, September through January in most of the United States; or infant nirsevimab. Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy; after a prior-pregnancy dose, the infant gets nirsevimab instead.
  • Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and varicella vaccines: live, contraindicated in pregnancy; if not immune, give after pregnancy, before discharge (varicella: a second dose 4 to 8 weeks later if never vaccinated).
  • Hepatitis B vaccine: if not already vaccinated, vaccinate in pregnancy (not PreHevbrio, which lacks pregnancy safety data).
  • Anti-D immunoglobulin: routinely at 28 weeks when Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen.
What is due now

The classic patient: Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen, non-immune to rubella, varicella immunoglobulin G (IgG) positive after a recent exposure, seen in mid-September.

Option analysis: why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhat kills it
Anti-D immunoglobulinShe is Rh-negative with a negative screenTiming: routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks
MMRShe is non-immune to rubellaLive, contraindicated; give after pregnancy, before discharge
TdapIndicated in every pregnancyTiming, as an optimization, not a gate: 27 to 36 weeks maximizes transplacental IgG transfer
Varicella vaccineRecent exposureLive, contraindicated, and she is already immune
Varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG)Exposure plus pregnancy is the classic postexposure prophylaxis settingVaricella IgG positive = immune; prophylaxis is for the non-immune

Two fail on timing, two on live-vaccine status, one on serology. Each distractor fails for a different reason: eliminate each on its own terms rather than comparing them.

Vaccines in pregnancy
RecommendedIf indicated or at riskNot in pregnancy
Inactivated influenza, seasonal; Tdap every pregnancy; RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks, September to January; hepatitis B if not already vaccinated (not PreHevbrio); anti-D at 28 weeks if Rh-negative with a negative antibody screenHepatitis A if at risk for infection or a severe outcome; meningococcal vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y if indicated; VZIG if exposed and non-immuneMMR, varicella, live attenuated influenza (LAIV), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guerin), oral polio: live vaccines are generally contraindicated. Human papillomavirus (HPV): not live, but deferred until after pregnancy. Recombinant zoster: no recommendation; consider delaying

No recommendation: pneumococcal vaccines (limited safety data) and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b). Newborns of mothers given the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine by mistake in pregnancy do not seem to be at increased risk.

COVID-19 ⚠︎: the CDC pregnancy table today gives no guidance, while the CDC 2026-2027 guidance recommends a COVID-19 vaccine for all adults 18 years and older; check the current schedule.

Anti-D immunoglobulin
Rh immunoglobulin timing 28 weeks routinely; within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive; any sensitizing event: vaginal bleeding, spontaneous or threatened abortion, ectopic or molar pregnancy, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma. A positive antibody screen without recent anti-D means she is already alloimmunized ⚠︎, so anti-D can no longer help: switch to titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler.
Varicella in pregnancy
Varicella in pregnancy Non-immune and exposed: VZIG as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Maternal varicella can cause varicella pneumonia (high mortality): intravenous acyclovir. Congenital varicella syndrome at 8 to 20 weeks (first or early second trimester; small risk, 0.4 to 2.0%): limb hypoplasia, cicatricial dermatomal scarring, chorioretinitis, cataracts. Neonatal varicella if the maternal rash occurs 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: VZIG to the newborn.
Practice
  1. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation asks which vaccines she needs First pregnancy; healthy, no medications Last Tdap at age 12 fetal heart tones present BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap at 27 to 36 weeks → Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, and the antibody transfer that protects the newborn is maximized at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably early in that window: schedule it; do not decline it. Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy, but a dose given earlier is not repeated in the window. Postpartum Tdap gives the infant no immunity. Give influenza vaccine now if it is in season
  2. 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation was exposed to chickenpox 3 days ago Her nephew's vesicular rash began the next day No history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination no rash Afebrile · varicella IgG negative → VZIG as soon as possible → a negative varicella IgG means she is not immune, so varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) is due: as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. Acyclovir treats varicella once the rash appears; it is not the prophylaxis here ⚠︎
  3. 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit in October She has had no influenza vaccine this season Healthy; takes only a prenatal vitamin Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Inactivated influenza vaccine today → no gestational window: inactivated influenza vaccine can be given at any time during pregnancy in the season, preferably September or October in the first or second trimester. Deferring to the third trimester leaves her unprotected through the season ⚠︎; the live attenuated vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy
  4. 23-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has had light vaginal bleeding since this morning Blood type A, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative closed cervix; fetal heart tones present HR 82/min · BP 114/70 mm Hg → Anti-D now, regardless of gestational age → vaginal bleeding is a sensitizing event, so anti-D is given now, regardless of gestational age; it is not held for the routine 28-week dose
  5. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation reviews her first prenatal labs Rubella IgG negative; varicella IgG positive asks whether she can be vaccinated against rubella now Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg → MMR postpartum before discharge → non-immune rubella is a classic stem: MMR is live and contraindicated in pregnancy, so give it after pregnancy, before discharge. It is not contraindicated for life
  6. 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation stepped on a rusty nail in her garden dirty puncture wound of the sole Last tetanus and diphtheria (Td) booster 12 years ago Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg → Tdap now → a tetanus-containing vaccine is indicated for this wound, and in a pregnant woman that dose is Tdap, given now: the window does not apply to prophylaxis. A dose given earlier in pregnancy is not repeated at 27 to 36 weeks
  7. 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has 4 days of a vesicular rash and 1 day of cough and dyspnea Her son had chickenpox 2 weeks ago T 38.4 °C · respiratory rate 28/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air → Varicella pneumonia → a varicella rash with dyspnea in pregnancy is varicella pneumonia, with high mortality: treat with intravenous acyclovir. Bacterial pneumonia would not explain the vesicular rash after a chickenpox exposure ⚠︎, and disseminated herpes zoster is a reactivation that begins in a dermatome, not a first infection after a chickenpox contact ⚠︎
  8. 26-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation in her first pregnancy comes for a visit in November She has not received a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine healthy Afebrile · BP 114/72 mm Hg → RSVpreF now → one dose of Abrysvo at 32 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks, September through January, protects the newborn; otherwise plan nirsevimab for the infant. Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, CDC does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy. The vaccine is recommended in pregnancy, not contraindicated
  9. 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Blood type B, Rh-negative No anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy antibody screen positive for anti-D BP 110/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 148/min → Antibody titers with serial MCA Dopplers → a positive antibody screen means she is already alloimmunized, and anti-D cannot undo it; follow titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler. Repeating the screen at 28 weeks only delays that surveillance ⚠︎
  10. 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Received Tdap at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy 2 years ago asks whether she needs it again BP 116/74 mm Hg · Afebrile → Give Tdap again → Tdap is given during each pregnancy, irrespective of a prior dose, because it protects this infant. Td lacks the pertussis component ⚠︎
  11. 21-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation asks about her human papillomavirus vaccine She received the first dose of a 3-dose series 2 months ago first prenatal visit BP 108/66 mm Hg · Afebrile → Defer to postpartum → HPV vaccines are not recommended in pregnancy; the rest of the series is delayed until the pregnancy is complete. The vaccine is not live and is not contraindicated for life; a dose given by mistake in pregnancy needs no intervention
  12. 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit Blood type O, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative Received Tdap at 27 weeks and influenza vaccine in October BP 116/72 mm Hg · fundal height 28 cm → Anti-D immunoglobulin → she is Rh-negative with a negative screen, and routine prophylaxis is due at 28 weeks. Tdap given earlier in this pregnancy is not repeated, and this season's influenza dose is done ⚠︎
  13. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation is offered the nasal influenza vaccine at a pharmacy in October No influenza vaccine this season healthy; no egg allergy Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine → the nasal formulation is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine, in any trimester during the season. Influenza vaccine is right; that influenza vaccine is wrong. Deferring vaccination entirely leaves her unprotected ⚠︎
  14. 26-year-old woman received MMR vaccine 3 weeks ago, then discovered she is pregnant Last menstrual period 7 weeks ago she asks whether the pregnancy is at risk Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Counsel and reassure; not an indication for termination → MMR inadvertently given in pregnancy: counsel her about the theoretical risk to the fetus; MMR vaccination during pregnancy is not a reason to terminate. The guidance calls for counseling about the theoretical risk, not fetal surveillance
  15. 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit Rh-negative; received anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks Rubella IgG negative; no Tdap yet this pregnancy BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap → Tdap is due in every pregnancy, optimally at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably early in that window, so 30 weeks is the time. Anti-D was given at 28 weeks. MMR is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give it after pregnancy, before discharge
  16. 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy term girl 1 day ago A vesicular rash appeared on her face and trunk 3 days before delivery No history of chickenpox mother T 37.8 °C · newborn HR 142/min → VZIG to the neonate → a maternal varicella rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery puts the newborn at risk: give varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) to the newborn. Maternal VZIG alone does not protect the newborn ⚠︎, and the live varicella vaccine is not the newborn's prophylaxis ⚠︎
  17. 34-year-old man asks about vaccines; his partner is at 32 weeks' gestation He has never received Tdap His mother, who will help care for the newborn, has not received it either Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Vaccinate them at least 2 weeks before contact → people who are not up to date should get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant (cocooning). Vaccinating after the birth leaves that first contact unprotected ⚠︎, and his partner's Tdap does not vaccinate the household ⚠︎
  18. 32-year-old woman is breastfeeding on the day after a vaginal delivery Rubella IgG negative on prenatal labs Received Tdap at 28 weeks; completed the HPV vaccine series at age 12 Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg → MMR → MMR after pregnancy, before discharge, for a patient without rubella immunity; it is safe while breastfeeding. Tdap is given immediately postpartum only when it was not given during pregnancy and she has never had Tdap, and her HPV series is complete
  19. 26-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 6-week-old son Rubella IgG and varicella IgG negative on prenatal labs asks whether vaccines are safe for her baby while she is nursing Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg → Inactivated and live vaccines are both permitted → neither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety, so MMR and varicella vaccine can be given now: the restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation. The exceptions are smallpox vaccine (contraindicated) and yellow fever vaccine (avoided unless travel cannot be postponed)
Why maternal Tdap Maternal Tdap is for the infant: the childhood pertussis series does not start until 2 months, and most infant pertussis deaths occur before that protection. It takes about 2 weeks after Tdap for the mother to be protected, and the antibody then needs time to cross, so late-third-trimester dosing is suboptimal; preterm delivery is the reason to dose at 27 weeks, not 36. Postpartum Tdap gives the infant no immunity. Household contacts who are not up to date get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant.
Breastfeeding The vaccine restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation: neither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety. Exceptions: smallpox vaccine is contraindicated and yellow fever vaccine is avoided unless travel cannot be postponed.
Common wrong answers Class versus member: influenza vaccine is right, but the live attenuated nasal one is wrong in pregnancy. Sequencing: Tdap today at 10 weeks, or deferred to postpartum, instead of scheduled at 27 to 36 weeks. Skipping Tdap because she had it last pregnancy: it is for this fetus.
Transferable rule

When a patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins, check the number (date, gestational age or titer) before weighing the indications. When a recommendation carries a time window, ask what it protects: if it optimizes an effect (antibody transfer), move outside it when the indication changes; if it defines eligibility (age 21 for cytology), you cannot.
